description: PhD candidate in artificial intelligence at Victoria University of Wellington. Deep learning for mass spectrometry and marine biomass analysis.

tagline: I apply deep learning to mass spectrometry so that fish can be identified, graded and traced by their chemistry.
about: I am a PhD candidate in artificial intelligence at Te Herenga Waka—Victoria University of Wellington. My thesis applies transformer models, self-supervised learning and explainable AI to rapid evaporative ionisation mass spectrometry (REIMS) data from the seafood industry.

Before the PhD I was a software engineer at NIWA, New Zealand's National Institute of Water and Atmospheric Research. I still think of code as a scientific instrument: something to build carefully, test and then point at an open question.
Off the clock I built a Skyrim-style wellbeing tracker and am currently lost somewhere in Baldur's Gate 3.

research.intro: The seafood industry needs fast, reliable answers about what a sample is, which part of the fish it came from, whether it has been contaminated and which batch it belongs to. My work replaces slow, expert-driven chemometrics with models that learn these answers directly from raw spectra.

highlights.detail: Transformer models reach 100% accuracy separating Hoki from Mackerel on REIMS spectra, against the OPLS-DA chemometric baseline.
An ensemble of transformers classifies seven body parts at 74.13% accuracy where OPLS-DA reaches 51.17%.
Ordinal classifiers detect graded oil contamination and cross-species mixing, with transfer learning improving contamination detection.
SpectroSim, a self-supervised contrastive method, identifies a sample's batch at 70.8% accuracy with no labels and no physical tags.
